title: Five-Clawed Dragon Robe

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Bequest of Duchesse de Richelieu, 1972
image.license: Public domain. Released under Creative Commons Zero (CC0) through the Met's Open Access program

altText: A long silk robe laid flat, with wide sleeves and a pattern of embroidered dragons and other ornament across the fabric.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record: title, objectDate, medium, period (Qing dynasty, 1644–1911), creditLine, classification (Costumes-Embroidered), tags (Dragons), public-domain flag, and image URLs read from the record

context: This silk robe was made in China during the Qing dynasty (1644-1911). Dragon robes were worn at the Qing court, and the number of claws on the dragons was part of a system of rank, with the five-clawed dragon reserved for the highest levels. The title of this robe refers to that five-clawed dragon design.

descriptions.k: This is a long silk robe with dragons on it. The dragons are stitched with thread. Find a dragon. Count its claws if you can. Is the robe plain or fancy?
descriptions.g12: This robe was made in China a few hundred years ago. It is made of silk and has dragons stitched on it. Dragons in this robe stand for power and good luck. Look for the dragons and the pattern around them. What would it be like to wear it?
descriptions.g35: This is a dragon robe from Qing dynasty China, made of silk. Court robes had dragons stitched on them, and the number of claws mattered: the five-clawed dragon was linked to the highest rank. Look for the dragons and other patterns on the robe. How do the dragons fill the shape of the robe? Why might clothing show rank this way?
descriptions.g68: Dragon robes were formal court dress in Qing China. The five-clawed dragon in the title refers to a rule of rank in which the number of claws helped signal who could wear a design. Embroiderers stitched dragons and symbolic patterns in silk thread, and the robe's wide shape displays them. How do the dragons guide your eye across the robe? What does clothing tell us about power and identity?
descriptions.g910: This 18th-century robe shows how clothing could communicate rank. In Qing court dress, dragon designs, including the five-clawed dragon, were regulated, so the garment is both costume and a visual code. The embroidered or woven patterns spread across a large silk surface, balancing dragons and other symbolic ornament. Consider how scale, repetition, and placement turn the robe into a statement of authority, and how wearing it differs from viewing it flat in a museum.
descriptions.g1112: As a Qing dragon robe, this garment belongs to a system of dress in which pattern functioned as rank. The five-clawed dragon of the title suggests high status, though the record gives no wearer, and sumptuary rules were not always applied rigidly. The robe thus raises questions about authority, display, and textile labor: what meanings were encoded in the dragons, who made and wore such garments, and how does displaying a robe flat change its meaning compared with a body in motion?

teacherNote.context: A Qing dynasty (18th century) silk dragon robe. The Met's title refers to five-clawed dragons, associated with the highest rank; the specific wearer is not recorded. Confirm visible colors and motifs from the image.
directions: Have students design a robe or banner using one animal to show a role, and explain their symbol.
Discuss how clothing communicates identity in schools, teams, and traditions around the world.
Compare this robe with the lotus robe in the archive to contrast dragon and flower imagery.
